```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5,
                      warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

Most diet questions are comparisons: before and after a change in the
ecosystem, small and large predators, one region and another. In DietView a
comparison starts with a covariate, a column you declare in `dv_spec()`. This
article shows how to build covariates from years and lengths, how to draw one
sunburst per level so the panels can be compared, and how to cross two
covariates.

The example table is invented and small: 24 records, 12 in each period. The
panels below show how a comparison is laid out. They are not evidence that
the diet changed.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

dat <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
```

## 1. Build covariates from years and lengths

`dv_add_period()` cuts years into periods and `dv_size_bins()` cuts lengths
into bins:

```{r helpers}
dv_add_period(c(2004, 2006, 2010, 2018), breaks = c(2003, 2007, 2020))
dv_size_bins(c(18, 26, 34, 52), breaks = c(0, 20, 30, 40, 60))
```

Two details decide which bin a value falls in. A year equal to an inner break
belongs to the earlier period (2007 falls in the first period above). A length
equal to an inner break belongs to the bin that starts there (30 cm falls in
the 30 to 40 bin), and a length at or beyond the last break gets no bin at all.
Choose breaks that cover every value you have:

```{r attach}
range(dat$somatic_length_cm)
dat$size_bin <- dv_size_bins(dat$somatic_length_cm, breaks = c(0, 30, 40, 50, 60, 100))
table(dat$size_bin, useNA = "ifany")
```

With `breaks = c(0, 40, 50, 60)` the 75 cm cod would have no size bin. A record
without a level is left out of that covariate's panels in the dashboard, and
shown in a separate "NA" panel in the Shiny app, so check the table above
before you go on. This `NA` is a missing stratum; it has nothing to do with the
unidentified prey in the sunburst.

Then declare the covariates and prepare the data:

```{r prep}
spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_species_common_name", stomach = "stomach_id",
                prey_id = "aphia_id", prey_name = "verified_name",
                weight = "prey_weight",
                covariates = c("period", "size_class", "size_bin", "region"))
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
```

## 2. One sunburst per period

Build one palette from all the records first, so that a taxon has the same
color in every panel:

```{r palette}
pal <- dv_palette(unlist(lapply(prep$ranks, function(r) prep$data[[r]])))
```

Then build one tree per level and draw each with that palette:

```{r periods}
d <- prep$data
periods <- sort(unique(d$period))
table(d$period)
```

```{r sunburst-p1}
t1 <- dv_build_tree(d[d$period == periods[1], ], prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(t1, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal, title = paste("Period", periods[1]))
```

```{r sunburst-p2}
t2 <- dv_build_tree(d[d$period == periods[2], ], prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(t2, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal, title = paste("Period", periods[2]))
```

How to read two panels side by side: both start at the same angle and list
taxa in the same order, so you read them in the same direction. A taxon does
not always sit at the same angle, though. If it is absent from one period,
every wedge after it moves round to close the gap. Use color, not position,
to find a taxon in both panels, and the hover labels to read its share.

To compare numbers rather than pictures, put the two rank tables side by side:

```{r compare}
cmp <- merge(dv_rank_table(t1, "Class")[, c("label", "pct_occ")],
             dv_rank_table(t2, "Class")[, c("label", "pct_occ")],
             by = "label", all = TRUE, suffixes = c("_p1", "_p2"))
cmp[is.na(cmp)] <- 0
cmp
```

Each column is a share of that period's records, unidentified records
included, so both columns add up to 100. With 12 records per period, a
difference of one record is a difference of more than 8 percentage points:
treat every difference here as noise. On real data, decide in advance how
many stomachs a panel needs before you interpret it, and report that number
with the figure.

## 3. Crossing two covariates

Often the question is size within period: does the diet of large predators
differ between periods in the same way as that of small ones? First count
what each combination holds:

```{r cross}
combos <- expand.grid(size = sort(unique(d$size_class)),
                      per  = sort(unique(d$period)),
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
combos$n_records  <- mapply(function(s, p) sum(d$size_class == s & d$period == p),
                            combos$size, combos$per)
combos$n_stomachs <- mapply(function(s, p)
  length(unique(d$stomach_id[d$size_class == s & d$period == p])),
  combos$size, combos$per)
combos
```

Crossing divides the sample quickly: here the juvenile cells hold two or
three records each. Draw a cell only when it holds enough stomachs to be
worth reading:

```{r cross-one}
sub <- d[d$size_class == "adult" & d$period == periods[1], ]
tc  <- dv_build_tree(sub, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(tc, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal,
            title = paste("adult,", periods[1]))
```

The Shiny app does the same interactively: choose a covariate under **Facet by
covariate** and a second one under **Cross with**, and it draws one panel per
combination (`run_dietview(prep)`).

## 4. All strata in one file

`dv_build_html()` writes every comparison into one HTML file: `strata` gives
each covariate its own row of sunbursts, and `cross` adds crossed rows.
`cross = list(c(inner, outer))` reads "inner within outer": one row per level
of `outer`, one sunburst per level of `inner` in that row.

```{r dash, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet_by_strata.html"),
              strata = c("period", "size_class", "size_bin"),
              cross  = list(c("size_bin", "period"),     # length bins within periods
                            c("size_class", "period")))  # size classes within periods
```

By default the build stays offline; see the species-cards article for
predator photos from iNaturalist, with their authors and licenses.
